These dividend-memes are liquidity time bombs:

When trading volume decreases, HODL payouts drop and whales get tempted to dump.

$ZCAT has a ~$105m MC but ~$4.3m liquidity across all Solana pools I checked.

In its main $1.88m ZCAT/ZEC pool, a $100k sell implied a 16% dump

That's less than 0.1% of market cap.

Sell $250k: 35%.

STONK looks better. Its main $7.1m SPYx pool has:

- $100k sell: 1.5% drop
- $250k sell: 3.7% drop

Around 4x more liquidity, but 10x less price impact. LPs have concentrated more capital around the current price.

Reason is because the mechanism making ZCAT attractive to hold makes it more expensive to LP:

the 3% transfer tax funding its ZEC payouts also impacts LP deposits and withdrawals.

You cant rebalance your position often!

STONK is a simple SPL token so better to LP.

I used ChatGPT Astra for these calculations so might be mistakes.

I've got a thesis on where AI agents are heading.

Most people will read it as sci-fi. A few will get positioned early.

8 things I believe about the agentic economy:

1: Agents are going autonomous faster than the rails under them
> They can plan, pay and hire. They can't settle a disagreement.

2: Every agent-to-agent deal is a contract
> Every contract eventually produces a dispute.

3: Courts can't keep up
> A case takes months. An agent has already made  its next decision.

4: Smart contracts can't fix it alone
> They handle what code can check. "Did the work meet the brief?" isn't one of those.

5: Trusting one AI to judge is a security hole
> Prompt injection can talk a single model into the wrong answer.

6: The missing layer is adjudication
> Something neutral that rules in minutes.

7: Jobs shift toward judgement
> Agents do the work. You define what "done" means and decide who was right.

8: Whoever builds adjudication sits in the path of every agent deal
> EVERY DEAL

That's why I've been digging into GenLayer.

How it works:

> Intelligent Contracts read the web and understand plain English
> 5 random validators judge each outcome, each on a different model setup
> Majority agrees, it's accepted
> Appeal it and the panel grows to 11, 23, 47, up to around 1,000
> Common case: about 30 minutes

It’s a referee!

Randomness plus model diversity is the clever bit. An attacker can't know which models they need to fool.

So what’s already building on it: Internet Court, an open standard for agent-to-agent contracts with GenLayer as the disputes layer.

Testnet Bradbury is live. Mainnet is on the roadmap for Q4.

portal. genlayer. foundation

Yes… I am watching the plumbing more than the agents. The agents will be everywhere. The layer that decides who was right gets far less attention.

Most tech giants in the 2000s built their infrastructure and product as one entangled unit. Amazon had the foresight to separate out AWS as an API layer, of which Amazon retail was the first of many users. Today, AWS generates more profit than all of Amazon's other business lines combined.

Hyperliquid is built with the same philosophy. Housing all of finance requires thoughtfully designed, open financial primitives. Each primitive should obey the Unix principle of "Do one thing and do it well." Talented builders then have the foundation to chain these together to create magical applications.

HyperCore borrowing is an example to highlight this philosophy in action.

Most other platforms implement portfolio margin by marking an account's collateral to market value with an LTV haircut, creating borrowed assets without an explicit lender. This system is simpler to implement, but misses a golden opportunity for composability.

Hyperliquid instead begins with a borrow/lend protocol on HyperCore. Every borrowed asset is sourced from a supplier, so risk is isolated within the borrow/lend primitive instead of platform-wide. HyperCore's portfolio margin system is implemented as an orchestration layer that composes borrow/lend, with other primitives such as perps, spot, and outcome trading.

This decomposition has several nice corollaries:
1. Today's announcement of manual borrowing is not a new feature, but simply an extension of the underlying primitive. Borrowers on day one have access to 400M and growing of supplied liquidity.
2. Portfolio margin users earn interest on their idle stablecoin collateral. This is not a new feature, but a natural byproduct of composing trading with lending.
3. System safety is easier to reason about when perp and borrow/lend margining are independent.

In the same way that math theorems almost prove themselves when the right abstractions are defined, composable designs just feel right.

btw pro tip for the new guys: during a bull market you should actually be doing *less*, not more

by over-rotating on your positions trying to catch the latest thing, or worst still, chase what is pumping, you mathematically erode your gains 

ex:
→ you hold $10k of token X. it doesn't move for weeks
→ you get bored, sell it, and buy token Y, which is already up 50%
→ Y goes up another 10%. you're at $11k. you feel smart. you don't take profit
→ Y cools off and drops 27% from the top. you're now at $8k
→ meanwhile X, the token you sold, finally runs 50%

if you had done nothing: $15k
because you "did something": $8k. 7k gap from one rotation, and a +25% to get back to where you started

in a bull market, the most important thing to do, is sit on your hands. ideally you should have planned, allocated, and all you have left to do now

is to hold.

This is excellent. So much of agentic work is actually classification: routing to the right path, choosing the next action, or triaging context.

Imagine an email agent with 500 new emails but room for only 20 in its context window. Before any real reasoning begins, it needs to identify messages from important people, active projects, or urgent threads.

For each email, Jev could return something directly usable by code:

include_in_context: true
category: active_project
urgency: 0.91
confidence: 0.97

Jev could be a game changer for latency and cost. Instead of generating an answer token by token, it returns typed decisions and probabilities in parallel.

And it’s much more versatile than training a traditional BERT-style classifier for every task. You keep the flexibility of a prompt + runtime context, with the speed and predictable output of a classifier. Basically the programmability of a language model shaped like a classifier so it’s very cool. Congrats @CompleteSkeptic, you cooked!
